stories.topic: Why the show is named after a Springsteen song
stories.summary: The title comes from Bruce Springsteen's 'You're Missing', from The Rising, the album he released after 9/11. In the song, someone moves through an apartment after a loved one has died in the attacks. The lyrics just list what is there: shirts in the closet, shoes in the hall, coffee cups on the counter, papers on the doorstep. Then: 'Everything is everything, but you're missing.' Amit plays it for his writing students to show that deep emotion needs no fancy adjectives or wordplay. The phrase also fits the show: both hosts refuse to see the world through one frame and want to stress how everything connects.
stories.insight: Plain, concrete detail can hit harder than ornament. The same banal-sounding phrase also works as a worldview about interconnectedness.
stories.quote: You don't need fancy adjectives or wordplay or whatever. Just a simple recounting of what is there and using simple terms can do it.

stories.topic: Nine more Murder in Mahim novels, written by AI
stories.summary: Amit recorded an eight-hour oral history with the writer Jerry Pinto for The Seen and the Unseen, which he calls perhaps his most memorable. He asked Pinto whether he would write more books after his crime thriller Murder in Mahim, and Pinto said no. Amit predicted that within a few years you could ask an AI to write nine more books in the series, and Pinto would not be able to tell the difference. He felt Pinto more or less agreed. Ajay later used that same conversation against him: no model trained on everything Pinto and Amit have ever said could reproduce what happened between them in that moment.
stories.insight: This is the whole debate in miniature. Continuing an existing style looks within a machine's reach. The live, one-time spark of a real encounter may not be.
stories.quote: a few years from now, you'll be able to tell an AI, write me nine more books in that series, and it will, and they'll be so good that Jerry will go, Wow, and he won't know the difference.

stories.topic: When engines got stronger, chess got more creative
stories.summary: Amit sets aside Kasparov's 1997 match against Deep Blue. For him the first real revolution came around 2003–04, when engines like Stockfish became clearly stronger than the best humans and players began training with them. People expected chess to become homogenized. Instead it diversified. The old Soviet-school heuristics about the centre, space and initiative had worked like a fixed rulebook, and engines exposed concrete exceptions to them. That freed players like Wesley So and Alireza Firouzja to think very differently. Anand once observed that in his generation a completely unexpected move was probably a bad one, while today's players simply think differently.
stories.insight: A powerful tool does not have to produce conformity. By exposing the exceptions to received wisdom, it can widen the space for creativity.
stories.quote: And instead of everything become homogenized because of computers, it actually went in the opposite direction.

stories.topic: AlphaZero replays chess history in a day, then leaves it behind
stories.summary: In 2017 AlphaZero taught itself chess in 24 hours, using no human games and only playing against itself. Its games retraced humanity's path. It took up the French Defence, fashionable in the 19th century and now seen as suboptimal, and it found the Berlin Defence that Kramnik unleashed against Kasparov. Then it went further. It rethought how much initiative is worth against material, and it launched flank attacks down the a- and h-files that Carlsen and others later adopted. Ajay added that it taught players not to rush to win back a sacrificed pawn: it is fine to take 15 moves if the sacrifice left a lasting structural weakness. Carlsen's coach Peter Heine Nielsen said he now knew how superior aliens would play. Yet how and why AlphaZero plays as it does remains a black box.
stories.insight: In a closed game with a clear reward, a machine can rediscover centuries of human knowledge and then move into territory we can watch but cannot explain.
stories.quote: I always wondered that if aliens with a superior intelligence came to Earth, how would they play chess? And now I know.

stories.topic: Machines break a 50-year record in matrix multiplication, then improve sorting
stories.summary: The best methods for multiplying matrices, Strassen-style algorithms, dated back about 50 years, and no human had improved on them. Researchers turned the problem into a game. They represented the multiplication algorithm itself as a parameter vector and optimised it for correctness and speed. The result was the first improvements in half a century, and these are now going into computer systems worldwide. DeepMind did the same with sorting code in LLVM, penalising mistakes and slowness, and found faster sorts. Mathematicians are now trying to understand the machine's discoveries and prove theorems about them.
stories.insight: Even the most basic operations in computing still had room to improve. The science-fiction spiral of machines building better machines is happening, in a quiet and mundane form, and it partners with human research rather than replacing it.
stories.quote: The machines are helping us to make a better sort algorithm. The machines are helping us to make a better matrix multiplication. And this feeds back to stronger machines.

stories.topic: Mary Wollstonecraft, Semmelweis and the unwashed hands
stories.summary: Mary Wollstonecraft read John Locke on natural rights and asked a simple question: why should they apply only to men? Her answer became A Vindication of the Rights of Woman. She died of an infection after childbirth, because doctors did not yet know they had to wash their hands. About half a century later, Ignaz Semmelweis showed that hand-washing prevented such deaths. For about twenty years he was ignored and hounded for defying convention, and he died in a mental asylum. Amit links this to Episode 1's discussion of the aggressively conventional-minded.
stories.insight: Conformity has a body count. Knowledge that could have saved lives was rejected for decades because it did not fit the consensus.
stories.quote: for about twenty years Semmelweis was ignored, he was hounded, he was cancelled because he did not conform to the conventional thinking, and he died in a mental asylum.

stories.topic: The daughter who invented a genre
stories.summary: The baby whose birth killed Wollstonecraft grew up, married Percy Shelley and became Mary Shelley. In her early twenties she wrote Frankenstein. It is often called the first science fiction novel; Amit prefers 'proto-science fiction'. Its monster has become a metaphor for many of today's fears about AI. Amit ties it back to the episode's argument: she created a genre with no precedent, the kind of leap no model trained on what came before would produce.
stories.insight: Mother and daughter form a remarkable arc, from 'why not women too?' to the first story about creating a monster. Mary Shelley is also a vivid example of genuinely new creation, the very thing the hosts were arguing about.
stories.quote: If you imagine her LLM, there is nothing like that. She's just creating this new genre, sui generis.

stories.topic: Nannari: one root, two journeys, one aha moment
stories.summary: On a Chennai street Ajay saw a man selling an unfamiliar root from a cart. Another customer rattled off its scientific name, Hemidesmus indicus. In Tamil it is nannari, smells of cardamom and camphor, and is made into an over-sugared syrup. Years later, hiking near Jivdan in the Sahyadris, he asked a village woman for ginger chai. She had no ginger and offered something else, and made a masala chai unlike any he had tasted. He voice-recorded the couple saying its Marathi name, and the husband dug him a sapling from the hillside. None of his Marathi-speaking friends recognised the name. Then one day, smelling the root, he realised it was the same plant as the Chennai nannari. He later found a Tamil Muslim tea recipe that uses it.
stories.insight: Local knowledge is scattered across languages and regions. Curiosity, careful records and patient triangulation turn two unrelated trips, years apart, into one story.
stories.quote: Then one fine day I was smelling that root and thinking and thinking, and I had that aha moment that this smell reminds me of Nannari, the Tamilian root that I had purchased in Chennai.

recommendations.item: You're Missing
recommendations.creator: Bruce Springsteen
recommendations.context: Explaining the show's name. The song is from The Rising, Springsteen's post-9/11 album.
recommendations.reason: It never fails to move him, and he uses it with writing students as a model of how simple, plain words can carry deep emotion.

recommendations.item: Do Not Go Gentle Into That Good Night
recommendations.creator: Dylan Thomas
recommendations.context: Ajay alludes to its 'rage, rage' line when describing the mood of the phrase 'everything is everything'.
recommendations.reason: He uses it as the contrast to his own stance: not raging against the world, but a quiet, confident, curious engagement with it.

recommendations.item: A Small-Sized Mystery
recommendations.creator: Jane Hirshfield
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes in the opening stretch, where Ajay says there are deep mysteries about human beings that science only dimly perceives. Not discussed on air.
recommendations.reason: A companion piece to the episode's point that much about human beings remains a mystery.

recommendations.item: Ajay Shah on how LLMs will impact us
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked alongside his argument that what passes for AI is really statistical models.
recommendations.reason: The longer written version of his view: LLMs are useful word-prediction tools that need a master's oversight, not intelligence.

recommendations.item: The War Against Cliche
recommendations.creator: Martin Amis
recommendations.context: Cited when Amit argues humans are also 'autocorrect on steroids'. He notes Amis had died recently.
recommendations.reason: A great collection of Amis's criticism. It is built around the fact that cliché is what writers most fear, which shows how much of human expression is autopilot.

recommendations.item: In a Silent Way (Episode 316 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Gaurav Chintamani
recommendations.context: Amit recalls Gaurav Chintamani, an immensely talented musician and producer, asking 'originality kya hai?'
recommendations.reason: A wonderful recent conversation in which a working artist questions whether originality even exists.

recommendations.item: The dialect of a cricket writer (2005)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Linked from his riff on cricket clichés like the 'elegant cover drive' and 'metronomic accuracy'.
recommendations.reason: His own catalogue of how sportswriting runs on stock phrases: human autocomplete in action.

recommendations.item: The Life and Times of Jerry Pinto (Episode 314 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Jerry Pinto
recommendations.context: His eight-hour conversation with Pinto, which Ajay holds up as something no LLM could recreate.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it perhaps his most memorable oral history.

recommendations.item: Murder in Mahim
recommendations.creator: Jerry Pinto
recommendations.context: The basis of Amit's prediction that AI will one day write convincing sequels.
recommendations.reason: He calls it a beautiful crime thriller.

recommendations.item: This century and the last one: A report card for the first 10 years (2010)
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes in the stretch where Ajay argues that the market economy has absorbed far bigger upheavals, like the steam engine and electricity.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's own long-horizon look at how the century was going. It is context for his calm about technological disruption.

recommendations.item: Discovering faster matrix multiplication algorithms with reinforcement learning
recommendations.creator: Alhussein Fawzi & others
recommendations.context: One of two recent results that had Ajay 'squealing with excitement'.
recommendations.reason: It produced the first improvements in about 50 years to one of computing's most basic operations, by turning algorithm design into a game.

recommendations.item: AlphaDev discovers faster sorting algorithms
recommendations.creator: DeepMind
recommendations.context: The companion example to the matrix-multiplication result.
recommendations.reason: It shows machines finding better code for something as fundamental as sorting, which then feeds back into stronger machines.

recommendations.item: The New World Upon Us (2017)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: The column he wrote after being blown away by AlphaZero.
recommendations.reason: His fuller account of why AlphaZero's self-taught chess was a turning point.

recommendations.item: Google's AlphaZero Destroys Stockfish In 100-Game Match
recommendations.creator: Mike Klein
recommendations.context: Linked in his account of AlphaZero surpassing Stockfish.
recommendations.reason: The contemporary report on the match that made AlphaZero famous.

recommendations.item: The Paperclip Maximizer
recommendations.context: Amit introduces the thought experiment as the classic example of AI alarmism.
recommendations.reason: An explainer of the scenario in which a machine built to maximise paperclips turns everything into paperclips.

recommendations.item: Why AI Will Save the World
recommendations.creator: Marc Andreeson
recommendations.context: Offered as the answer to fears that AI will wipe out humanity.
recommendations.reason: In Amit's words, a beautiful essay that addresses all of these questions in great detail.

recommendations.item: When We Were Robots in Egypt
recommendations.creator: Jo Walton
recommendations.context: Ajay, calling 'machines will rule the world' claims science-fiction material, says there are beautiful poems about this and promises to link one.
recommendations.reason: A literary take on the machines-take-over theme he finds farcical as a forecast but beautiful as art.

recommendations.item: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
recommendations.creator: Mary Wollstonecraft
recommendations.context: The first of his three linked recommendations.
recommendations.reason: A classic of feminism he holds close to his heart. It applies Locke's natural rights to women, and works as both philosophy and polemic.

recommendations.item: Frankenstein
recommendations.creator: Mary Shelley
recommendations.context: The second recommendation, written by Wollstonecraft's daughter.
recommendations.reason: A pioneering, sui generis work of proto-science fiction written in her early twenties. Its monster speaks to today's fears about AI.

recommendations.item: Romantic Outlaws
recommendations.creator: Charlotte Gordon
recommendations.context: The third recommendation, which ties the first two together.
recommendations.reason: It tells the lives of Wollstonecraft, Mary Shelley and their circle. Amit finds these beautiful and inspiring lives.

recommendations.item: The poetry of Mary Oliver
recommendations.creator: Mary Oliver
recommendations.context: Amit says Shelley, Byron and Keats are overrated and kill young people's passion for poetry.
recommendations.reason: What schools should be teaching instead of the Romantic poets.

recommendations.item: The poetry of Mark Strand
recommendations.creator: Mark Strand
recommendations.context: Paired with Mary Oliver as a replacement for the Romantics in school.
recommendations.reason: The other poet he would teach instead.

recommendations.item: Amit Varma's Book Club episodes on A Vindication of the Rights of Woman and Frankenstein (Storytel)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: He did roughly 15-minute audio episodes on both books for Storytel.
recommendations.reason: Short audio introductions to the two books he recommends.

recommendations.item: The Art of Clear Writing
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Ajay says Amit's writing course would never include a session on getting ChatGPT to write for you.
recommendations.reason: It stands for the craft Ajay prizes: fighting for every word and every phrase on the road to mastery.

recommendations.item: Saaya & the Rituals of Tamil Muslim Milk Tea
recommendations.creator: Maazin Buhari
recommendations.context: Ajay found that nannari chai is a Tamil Muslim recipe and that the recipe is online.
recommendations.reason: The source for the recipe behind his 'better masala chai'.

recommendations.item: Nannari root (Amrutmul, Hemidesmus indicus)
recommendations.context: His recommendation for the episode: grind the root into powder and add it to masala chai.
recommendations.reason: It gives a novel, unique flavour with hints of cardamom and camphor that most masala-chai lovers north of Karnataka have never tried.

core_ideas.concept: Everything is everything: many frames, calm engagement
core_ideas.explanation: The world's incentives push people to specialise and narrow. Understanding the world and acting in it needs interdisciplinary thinking that pulls diverse tools together. Ajay adds a temperament to this. Look at the world calmly and curiously, without rage, and sustain your energy like a marathon runner rather than burning out in fury.
core_ideas.quote: I think it's an essential part of all of us that we have to be marathon runners. The world is hard, the world is complicated, and there is no point in screaming.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay argues the word 'AI' smuggles in the idea of fluid, creative, purposeful human intelligence. What exists today is statistical models, which are powerful and useful but limited. A model that flags TB on X-rays is valuable, but it is not general intelligence. He is a materialist and sees nothing mystical in the skull. Still, the urge that makes us wake up and decide to build something new is beyond any LLM.
core_ideas.quote: Everything that passes for AI in this world are really statistical models that are processing data.

core_ideas.concept: AI is whatever hasn't become normal yet
core_ideas.explanation: Once a technology becomes commonplace, we stop calling it AI. Computers, the internet and GPS all followed this path; a friend of Amit's notes that young people will never know what it is like to get lost. Ajay's example is Ken Thompson's dynamic-programming solution to chess endgames, a thunderbolt at first and now taken for granted.
core_ideas.quote: we'll call something AI till it becomes commonplace in part of our lives and then we just treat it as commonplace, as normalized. We don't call it AI anymore.

core_ideas.concept: Creativity seems mystical only because we can't see its mechanism
core_ideas.explanation: Amit argues against human hubris. Art and craft are the same thing; art just feels mystical because we don't know how our neurons produce it. Humans run on far less training data and processing power than modern models. Dismissing AI now is like dismissing computing in 1950 because mainframes filled rooms.
core_ideas.quote: I'm saying Beethoven's brain had nothing but statistical models, and that's enough to reach that level of creativity.

core_ideas.concept: Humans are autocomplete on steroids too
core_ideas.explanation: The jibe that LLMs are 'just autocomplete' applies to us as well. Writers fear cliché above all, and everyday speech runs on stock phrases: every cover drive is 'elegant', every accurate bowler has 'metronomic accuracy'. Even a gifted musician like Gaurav Chintamani wonders whether originality exists at all.
core_ideas.quote: a common criticism against LLM is that hey, these are autocorrect on steroids, right? Of course they are. So are we.

core_ideas.concept: The Einstein test: derivative vs genuinely new
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's case for human uniqueness goes like this. Stand in 1905 with every text in the world, and no LLM under any prompting scheme produces special relativity. A model trained on Akbar's tomb at Sikandra would never invent the Taj Mahal. Models trained on the past stay derivative. Amit's rejoinder is that this is an argument about LLMs, not about AI as a whole.
core_ideas.quote: if your corpus never had special relativity, no LLM will ever invent special relativity.

core_ideas.explanation: Divide workers into quartiles, from Q1 (weakest) to Q4 (masters). LLMs, trained on the internet's mix of gems and garbage and prone to hallucination, can lift Q2 workers to roughly Q3 output. But a master must always check and approve the result. Ajay calls this a tool made in heaven for India, which has few masters and many weak workers, provided management techniques are built around it.
core_ideas.quote: The product has to always be approved by a master. The product can never be approved by a junior.

core_ideas.concept: Shortcuts can contaminate the journey to mastery
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's real worry is not job loss but apprenticeship. If GitHub Copilot finishes your code and ChatGPT drafts your prose, you may never build the problem-solving or writing craft that mastery requires. Is that like the calculator making arithmetic skill obsolete? Ajay thinks not, and would switch off Copilot if he were 17. Amit counters that only a small, self-motivated minority ever pursues mastery, and they will get there anyway. The rewards for mastery are now far bigger.
core_ideas.quote: So I see it as contaminating the journey to mastery. Okay, we all start out as journeymen and we get stronger.

core_ideas.explanation: Thin desire is wanting market success and validation for your work. Thick desire is the joy of creating and mastery for its own sake. Amit expects AI eventually to churn out great novels, music and operas that no human can compete with commercially. Creators who work for the act itself lose nothing. Those who work for validation were doing it for the wrong reason anyway.
core_ideas.quote: What will remain with you is the joy of creation, the mastery for its own sake, for the satisfaction it gives you.

core_ideas.concept: Mass production dies, true originality wins big
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay expects AI to wipe out paid human work on formulaic output: romance novels, stock screenplays, mass-produced research papers and op-eds. He sees a winner-takes-all world in which a few humans produce true originality and machines make the rest. Amit expects copywriting and illustration jobs to shrink in the same way. Both hosts doubt this means long-run unemployment. Amit expects the productivity gains to flow back into the economy. Ajay notes that markets absorbed the steam engine and electricity, calling this 'small change' by comparison.
core_ideas.quote: You don't need a creative director with ten copywriters. You need a creative director who can prompt.

core_ideas.concept: Turn it into a game: machine discovery in closed problems
core_ideas.explanation: When a problem has fixed rules and an objective reward, as in chess, protein folding, matrix multiplication or sorting, machines can climb toward better solutions and find genuinely new things rather than remixing the past. This is what excites Ajay most. He sees these tools partnering with humans and changing how knowledge is produced. But most real-world problems are messy statistical inference under uncertainty, where errors never go away.
core_ideas.quote: the beauty is chess is a finite game with reward function, and you're able to climb that hill and discover new wonders by climbing the hill, and you're not just derivative.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit presents the paperclip maximizer, a machine that turns the universe into paperclips, as the classic alarmist scenario, and rejects it twice over. First, he asks why we place the human species on a pedestal at all. Second, he thinks it simply won't happen, any more than GPS will destroy us. Ajay calls machine-takeover claims farcical, the stuff of science fiction.
core_ideas.quote: why are we placing the human species on a pedestal if it wipes us out, it wipes us out.

core_ideas.concept: The real AI risks are mundane: Type I vs Type II errors
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay compares AI to the automobile: accidents happen, and we blame the driver, not the car. Diagnostic algorithms will kill people through mistakes, and military robots will kill civilians; he says this will happen 'with probability one'. Every system trades off false alarms against misses. Society settles the weights through liability, regulation or industry norms, and Ajay wants to be 'fully Coasean' rather than leave it all to government. Amit adds a 'seen and unseen' point: we see the lives an algorithm costs, but not the lives it saves.
core_ideas.quote: So all engineering involves finding a design that finds an ethical, legal, and safe trade-off between type one and type two errors.

core_ideas.concept: Man-machine hybrids, and how long they last
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's ideal for diagnosis is a hybrid. The machine confidently clears the obvious cases and sends the uncertain middle to an expensive human master. Firms will be tempted to cut corners on that master. Amit warns that chess experts once confidently said a human-plus-engine team would beat either alone. Ajay replies that chess is a finite, closed problem, while real-world inference always carries error.
core_ideas.quote: today we look back on that and with hindsight, we can say that it is ludicrous.

core_ideas.explanation: Most people extend moral consideration only to humans, and often only to some humans, partly because they see themselves as more intelligent and conscious. Amit asks what happens if an AGI is smarter than us and has some analogue of consciousness. Being flesh and blood and mortal seems a thin basis for keeping it enslaved. Ajay declines the premise; until AGI with consciousness exists, the ethics is ordinary engineering.
core_ideas.quote: Why should I be your slave? I'm superior to you in every way, I'm smarter in every way and I'm not going to die.

core_ideas.concept: Dietary biodiversity as respect for our ignorance
core_ideas.explanation: For most of modern humans' roughly 100,000 years, we lived as hunter-gatherers eating hundreds of species. Science only found vitamins in the 20th century; scurvy on long sea voyages was solved simply by carrying pickled limes. Our grasp of micronutrients and the body is still thin. So eating a wide diversity of species, and drawing on traditional knowledge, hedges against what we don't know.
core_ideas.quote: the sheer number of different species that you're taking in is a way of respecting our lack of knowledge about the way the human body works.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Told by the producer to drop his 'resting pout face', Amit promises a 'jokerish permanent smile' for the rest of the episode. Then: 'Maybe a joker mask will work.'
Amit: 'we of course are artists as we discussed in the last episode. That was an allegation made on us.'

Ajay imagines an LLM reading everything the two hosts have written, guessing 'that we are nutcases', and arriving at the name Everything is Everything. That, he says, would be the pinnacle of word prediction.

Amit on protein folding: 'if you've ever seen me wrap a piece of bacon around a sausage, you'll realize I'm bloody good at protein folding.' He then asks Ajay, who had described 'squealing with excitement', to actually demonstrate a squeal.
Amit on Mary Wollstonecraft: 'Married to an interesting guy, also a bit of an asshole, but leave him out of the equation.'
Amit closes the AI debate: they 'agree to disagree genially, as AI also would, because no emotions — we are the messed up creatures.'
Ajay's wife Susan says his herbal 'tea' isn't tea at all, because there's no tea in it.

The 'third host' is Mark, who cavorted in the background and fell asleep on a bookshelf. The producers said they hadn't heard a word the hosts said 'because you're old and boring anyway', only that Mark was there. Ajay: 'Mark has more AGI than any LLM.' Amit: 'I don't even know what you mean by that.'
Hemingway, quoted by Ajay on the craft of writing: 'a good day is one in which you write one good sentence.'

Ken Thompson's dynamic-programming algorithm for chess endgames. Ajay: it was 'like a thunderbolt going off' when it arrived and is 'boring' today, an eerie thing that 'looks 20 deep without needing 20 ply.'
Idealism vs materialism: Ajay puts himself 'on the materialism side. There is nothing happening in the skull other than some quantum mechanics of how the atoms in this brain work.'
Amit invokes the old idea that enough monkeys will eventually type Shakespeare, as a way to think about AI matching great creative work.
Ajay's architecture analogy: a model standing at Akbar's tomb in Sikandra would never invent the Taj Mahal, the next step in 'the great arms race of monuments'.
Amit, deflating human exceptionalism: 'some would of course argue we are colonized by bacteria, we're colonized by wheat.'
Ajay: if you grant conscious AGI, 'then we're building von Neumann machines. We're colonizing the galaxy.'
Ajay on AI regulation: 'I want to be fully Coasean. You don't have to have governments doing all the heavy lifting.'

Amit's hot take on the Romantic poets Shelley, Byron and Keats: they 'should not even be taught in school' because 'they take away young people's passion for poetry. They're not even good poets, we romanticize them.'
